newsitem.title: UK: UK's FTSE 100 posts biggest percent drop since '92.
newsitem.headline: UK's FTSE 100 posts biggest percent drop since '92.

text.p: Britain's leading share index on Friday posted its largest percentage drop since October 1992, falling 2.5 percent as investors locked in their profits after a record-run this month.

A steep early selloff on Wall Street and share declines in banking powerhouse HSBC Holdings, down seven percent, and oil companies, also left the FTSE 100 index with a loss of 165.5 points on the week.
The FTSE 100 finished 125.5 points lower at 4,865.8, down from its all-time best of 5,095.3 hit last week which is 24 percent higher than it was at the end of 1996.
But volume was light on Friday at around 745 million shares though decliners led advancers by 89 to 11.
The Dow was down 124 points in early action, then trimmed those losses by the London close, to trade 78.28 points lower at 7,863.75 by 1607 GMT.
The London sell-off was exacerbated by the thin summer activity, with holidays across Europe, and the expiry of index options, market sources said.
Yet the broader index was higher as investors continued to buy the second-tier industrial firms that underperformed this year when sterling was at higher levels.
The strong currency raised fears that their overseas earnings would be hit when profits are translated back into sterling.
The FTSE 250 index gained 8.3 points or 0.18 percent to 4,698.2, a gain of nearly 50 points on the week.
"People are looking to switch out of the main line and into the second line stocks," said Brian O'Donnell, sales trader at Schroders.
"I think the local options traders, with the index option expiry and with people away, are taking the opportunity to bang the market up," he said.
Shares in HSBC, Asia's biggest bank, tumbled 165p to 21.69 pounds in London, tracking a selloff in Hong Kong.
Investors fretted over Asian currency woes and fears that speculators would build up positions against the Hong Kong dollar, potentially hurting profits of banks in that market.
Standard Chartered Plc, another bank with a big Asia-Pacific franchise, lost 37-1/2p to 10.15 stg.
"Looking around it seems as if people are playing the currency card," one analyst said.
"If it is profit taking on top of that, then there will be more taken out of HSBC than Standard Chartered because it has recently outperformed more," he said.

British Petroleum shares were also heavy losers, tracking a selloff in their American Depository Receipts, where they were among the most actively traded on the New York Stock Exchange overnight and on Friday morning.
A sharp sell-off in the futures market also weighed on the cash index, traders said, with the September contract valued at a discount to the cash market.
"Volumes are very thin and the futures are very weak," one trader said.
"It's just a case of us drifting down from 5,100 and the buyers are waiting," he said. "If you look at the volume it's not great, which suggests to me it's just a buyers' strike."
